title: The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance
title_zh: 委托困境：规模经济、问责制与多中心治理

paragraphs.en: M. Baldoni, F. Fang, W. Yeoh, N. Yorke-Smith (eds.) \submissionType Research Paper Track
paragraphs.zh: M. Baldoni, F. Fang, W. Yeoh, N. Yorke-Smith（编）\submissionType 研究论文赛道

sents.en: M. Baldoni, F. Fang, W. Yeoh, N.

paragraphs.en: Many collective-action systems are neither fully decentralized nor fully centralized: agents voluntarily organize into institutions that share organizational costs and delegate decisions to representatives. Delegation can reduce individual costs, but it also transfers control to representatives whose private objectives need not align with those of their constituents. We study this tension in a repeated game with endogenous delegation to self-interested centers. A simple reduced-form model yields a scale–accountability tradeoff : larger constituencies offer greater cost-sharing benefits to members, yet the marginal value to a center of retaining any one constituent decreases as group size grows. Consequently, the prospect of individual exit can sustain non-exploitative delegation only up to an endogenous accountable constituency size. Additionally, we identify parameter regions in which fully delegated, accountable governance, when feasible, must be polycentric . We investigate these predictions through simulations with large language model (LLM) agents. Across five matched pairs of 30-agent simulations, polycentric structures repeatedly emerge but remain fluid, exhibiting cycles of concentration, exploitation, exit, and re-formation. We further find that models of different capacity exhibit similar willingness to assume leadership but differ substantially in their exercise of authority, with Sol initiating exploitation more frequently than Luna in matched decision states.
paragraphs.zh: 许多集体行动系统既不是完全去中心化的，也不是完全中心化的：智能体自愿组织成机构，以分摊组织成本并将决策委托给代表。 委托可以降低个体成本，但也会把控制权转移给代表，而代表的私人目标未必与其选民的目标一致。 我们在一个允许向自利中心进行内生委托的重复博弈中研究这种张力。 一个简化的简约式模型给出了规模与问责之间的权衡：更大的选民群体能为成员提供更大的成本分摊收益，但随着群体规模扩大，中心从保留任何一个选民中获得的边际价值却会下降。 因此，个体退出的前景只能在某个内生的可问责选民规模之内维持非剥削性的委托关系。 此外，我们识别出这样一些参数区域：在其中，完全委托且可问责的治理在可行时必然是多中心的。 我们通过使用大语言模型（LLM）智能体的仿真来检验这些预测。 在五组各含 30 个智能体的配对仿真中，多中心结构反复出现但仍保持流动，呈现出集中、剥削、退出与重组的循环。 我们进一步发现，不同能力水平的模型在承担领导角色的意愿上相似，但在行使权力方面差异显著：在配对的决策状态中，Sol 发起剥削的频率高于 Luna。

paragraphs.en: Socially valuable activities often exhibit economies of scale : they are costly, or even infeasible, when undertaken individually, but become easier to perform as individuals organize into groups. Farmers may cooperate in production or irrigation, fishers may jointly manage a common resource, and communities may pool resources to provide local public services. Such activities naturally give rise to constituencies, with organizers or leaders who coordinate contributions, make collective decisions, and determine how the gains from cooperation are distributed. The benefits of scale have long been central to theories of clubs and collective action ( Buchanan, 1965 ; Ostrom et al., 1961 ) , as well as to more recent work on endogenous group formation ( Page et al., 2005 ; Ahn et al., 2008 ) .
paragraphs.zh: 具有社会价值的活动往往表现出规模经济：个体单独从事这些活动代价高昂，甚至不可行，但当个体组织成群体后，活动就会变得更容易开展。 农民可以在生产或灌溉方面合作，渔民可以共同管理一种公共资源，社区可以汇集资源以提供地方公共服务。 此类活动自然会催生利益群体，由组织者或领导者来协调各方贡献、作出集体决策，并决定合作收益如何分配。 规模带来的好处长期以来一直是俱乐部理论与集体行动理论（Buchanan, 1965; Ostrom et al., 1961）的核心，也是近期关于群体内生形成研究的核心（Page et al., 2005; Ahn et al., 2008）。

paragraphs.en: At the same time, organizational scale may alter the incentives of those entrusted with authority. As a constituency grows, the centre’s marginal organizational benefit from retaining any particular constituent may decline. A self-interested centre may therefore find it profitable to exploit some delegates, even when doing so risks their eventual departure. When losing a constituent has only a small effect on the centre’s future organizational costs, the threat of exit provides a weaker deterrent against exploitation. Thus, the same economies of scale that encourage collective organization can also undermine the accountability of those exercising delegated authority and create scope for opportunism. This tension echoes the classical observation that organizational growth can concentrate decision-making authority ( Michels, 1915 ) .
paragraphs.zh: 与此同时，组织规模可能会改变那些受托掌握权力者的激励。 随着选民群体扩大，中心从保留任何一个特定选民中获得的边际组织收益可能会下降。 因此，一个自利的中心可能会发现剥削某些代表是有利可图的，即使这样做有他们最终离开的风险。 当失去一个成员对中心未来的组织成本只有很小影响时，退出的威胁对剥削行为的威慑作用就会减弱。 因此，鼓励集体组织的规模经济同样可能削弱行使被授予权力者的问责性，并为机会主义创造空间。 这一张力呼应了一个经典论断，即组织增长可能使决策权集中（Michels, 1915）。

sents.zh: 与此同时，组织规模可能会改变那些受托掌握权力者的激励。

paragraphs.en: However, such opportunism does not necessarily imply the persistence of a single governing authority. Constituents who receive an exploitative treatment can instead exercise exit ( Hirschman, 1970 ) , by joining an alternative constituency or by volunteering to lead a new constituency themselves. Competition for constituents therefore constraints the size of the groups and their leaders’ ability to benefit at the expense of their members. At the same time, groups cannot become arbitrarily small, because doing so sacrifices the economies of collective production. The resulting institutional structure is therefore neither individual nor fully centralized, but polycentric : multiple, relatively autonomous centers of organization coexist, compete for constituents, and may cooperate where doing so is mutually beneficial. This conception is closely related to the polycentric political systems of Ostrom, Tiebout, and Warren ( Ostrom et al., 1961 ) , and to Ostrom’s later account of polycentric governance as an alternative to the dichotomy between centralized state provision and purely decentralized market exchange ( Ostrom, 1990 ) . Examples of polycentricity are also prevalent in practice. For example, in experiments with members of Chilean territorial-use-right fisheries, Chávez et al. ( Chávez et al., 2023 ) find that while fishers frequently formed the grand coalition when monitoring was inexpensive, in fully decentralized settings without monitoring, the former coalitions were many more and significantly smaller. Thus, our general aim in this paper is to study and understand the following phenomenon: polycentricity arises not merely because different tasks are efficiently performed at different scales, but because organizational scale itself changes the incentives of those entrusted with authority.
paragraphs.zh: 然而，这种机会主义并不必然意味着单一治理权威的持续存在。 受到剥削对待的成员可以选择退出（Hirschman, 1970），即加入另一个可供选择的成员群体，或者自愿领导建立一个新的成员群体。 因此，对成员的竞争限制了群体的规模，也限制了其领导者以牺牲成员利益为代价谋取私利的能力。 与此同时，群体也不能变得任意小，因为这样做会牺牲集体生产的规模经济。 由此形成的制度结构既不是个体的，也不是完全集中的，而是多中心的：多个相对自主的组织中心并存，彼此竞争成员，并在互利的情形下可能开展合作。 这一概念与 Ostrom、Tiebout 和 Warren 的多中心政治系统（Ostrom et al., 1961）密切相关，也与 Ostrom 后来将多中心治理作为集中式国家供给与纯粹分散式市场交换这一二分法之外的替代方案（Ostrom, 1990）密切相关。 多中心性的例子在实践中也很普遍。 例如，在对智利领海使用权渔业成员的实验中，Chávez 等人 （Chávez et al., 2023）发现，虽然当监督成本较低时渔民经常形成大联盟，但在没有监督的完全分散的环境中，联盟数量要多得多且规模明显更小。 因此，本文的总体目标是研究和理解以下现象：多中心性的产生，不仅仅是因为不同的任务在不同规模下能够被高效执行，更是因为组织规模本身会改变被赋予权威者的激励。

paragraphs.en: With the rapid development and employment of AI systems, individuals and organizations increasingly delegate their decisions to autonomous AI agents, and in particular to agents powered by large language models that act on their behalf. A growing literature has already begun to examine delegation to artificial agents in collective-action environments, e.g., see ( Domingos et al., 2022 ; Nguyen et al., 2025 ; Faulkner et al., 2026 ) . This raises the question of whether the institutional forces that generate polycentricity among human decision makers continue to operate when such decisions are delegated to AI agents. Will AI agents recognize the economic advantages of delegation and voluntarily form constituencies? How will self-interested AI centres exercise their authority as constituency size increases? Can the prospect of losing constituents discipline exploitation, or will centres anticipate that departing members can be replaced? Will agents establish competing centres when existing governance arrangements become unattractive? Finally, will different language models respond similarly to the same institutional incentives, or exhibit distinct patterns in their exercise of delegated authority?
paragraphs.zh: 随着人工智能系统的快速发展和投入使用，个人和组织日益将决策委托给自主的智能体，尤其是委托给代表其行事、由大语言模型驱动的智能体。 越来越多的文献已经开始研究在集体行动环境中向人工智能体的委托，例如参见（Domingos et al., 2022；Nguyen et al., 2025；Faulkner et al., 2026）。 这就提出了一个问题：当此类决策被委托给智能体时，那些在人类决策者中产生多中心性的制度力量是否仍会继续发挥作用。 智能体会认识到委托的经济优势并自愿组成选民群体吗？ 随着选民群体规模的扩大，自利的智能体中心将如何行使其权力？ 失去选民的前景能否约束剥削行为，还是各中心会预期离开的成员能够被替换？ 当现有的治理安排变得缺乏吸引力时，智能体会建立相互竞争的中心吗？ 最后，不同的语言模型对相同的制度激励会作出相似的反应，还是在行使被委托的权力时表现出不同的模式？

paragraphs.en: More generally, we are interested to know whether interactions among autonomous AI agents reflect the endogenous checks on organizational scale that sustain polycentricity among human decision makers, or whether they instead generate qualitatively different organizational structures. Our aim is therefore not to assume that polycentricity is a stable outcome, but to understand the institutional incentives that make it possible and the strategic behaviour that shapes its emergence and persistence.
paragraphs.zh: 更一般地说，我们关心的是自主人工智能智能体之间的互动，是反映了维系人类决策者之间多中心性的对组织规模的内在制约，还是会生成性质上不同的组织结构。 因此，我们的目标不是假定多中心性是一种稳定的结局，而是理解使其成为可能的制度激励，以及塑造其出现与延续的策略行为。

paragraphs.en: We study whether polycentric arrangements emerge among autonomous LLM agents, how they evolve as constituencies gain and lose members, and whether different models exercise delegated authority in similar ways. Our main contributions are as follows:

paragraphs.en: (i) We develop a general model of voluntary delegation, economies of scale, and exit-based accountability (Figure 1 ). Our model is deliberately stylized, and intentionally abstracts away from the particulars of the task (e.g., whether it is a resource harvesting task or any other task) and the form of exploitation (e.g., whether that arises via some misallocation of resources etc). The aim of the model is to capture the fundamental tension between the efficiency gains from forming larger groups and the centers’ incentives for exploitation, and the conditions under which this leads to polycentric structures. Participation depends on the average-cost saving created by joining a constituency, whereas accountability depends on the marginal organizational value that the center loses when one constituent exits. We derive a minimum viable constituency size, a maximum size at which probabilistic individual exit can deter exploitation, comparative statics, and an exact characterization of the number of centers compatible with fully delegated accountable governance. A fixed-cost specialization yields closed-form thresholds. Our theoretical results serve as baselines to ground our simulations.

paragraphs.en: (ii) We study endogenous governance formation among Large Language Model (LLM) agents . Across ten matched episodes with 30 agents, polycentric structures repeatedly emerge through both bottom-up formation and fragmentation of concentrated authority, but remain fluid as fee sharing attracts agents toward larger constituencies and exploitation induces exit. We additionally compare GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6 Sol (small vs. large model) pointwise on the same post-initialisation decision states. The two models are similarly willing to become centers but differ substantially in how they exercise delegated authority, with Sol initiating exploitation more often under matched conditions.

Our model connects work on club and coalition formation with delegation and institutional accountability. Classical club theory studies how cost sharing and congestion determine desirable group size ( Buchanan, 1965 ) , while coalition-formation models study the endogenous emergence and stability of group structures ( Ray and Vohra, 1999 ; Page et al., 2005 ; Ahn et al., 2008 ) . Most closely related to our dynamic setting, Joshi (2025) studies sequential club formation when agents’ preferences depend on club size. Endogenous group formation has also been studied in collective-resource settings ( Chávez et al., 2023 ) and in environments with multiple centrally coordinated groups ( Harlalka et al., 2023 ; Harlalka and Griffin, 2025 ) . Our upper size limit has a different source: larger groups dilute the disciplinary effect of losing any particular member rather than generating congestion or technological inefficiency.

A second line of literature studies delegation to representatives or intermediaries. Hamman et al. (2011) show experimentally that groups may voluntarily delegate public-good decisions to elected members, and that poorly performing representatives can subsequently be replaced. Related work studies representation in public-good games ( Hauge and Røgeberg, 2015 ; Hamman et al., 2010 ) , delegation as a coordination mechanism ( Corazzini et al., 2020 ) , and delegation of common-pool-resource decisions to a stakeholder ( Bayle et al., 2024 ) . Our distinctive mechanism combines voluntary constituency formation with a self-interested center whose incentive to retain each constituent decreases with organizational scale. This links economies of scale directly to exit-based accountability.

Finally, recent work studies institutional mechanisms among LLM agents. Faulkner et al. (2026) introduce elected leadership in LLM social groups, while Tewolde et al. (2026) compare repetition, reputation, mediation, and contracting as cooperation-sustaining mechanisms. Hierarchical authority, elections, and oversight have also been studied in LLM public-good environments ( Seyedin et al., 2026 ) . Rather than imposing a fixed governance institution, we ask whether self-interested AI agents endogenously form centralized, polycentric, or individual governance structures when organizational scale simultaneously creates economic benefits and weakens accountability.

Theorem 13 is a feasibility and necessity result, not an equilibrium-selection claim. It identifies a region, under benchmark conditions, in which economies of scale rule out very small delegated institutions while accountability rules out a grand center . Whether decentralized strategic agents discover and sustain such structures once formation and replacement evolve endogenously is the question we examine experimentally.

Our theory characterizes when accountable delegation requires authority to be distributed across multiple centers. Such structural polycentricity , however, does not necessarily imply diversity in how those centers behave. We therefore distinguish between structural polycentricity, which describes the distribution of authority across centers, and behavioural diversity , which describes whether distinct centers make different decisions when facing comparable strategic conditions. In simple terms, a system can be highly polycentric in its formal organization while remaining behaviourally concentrated if its centers respond similarly to the same situations. This distinction is particularly relevant when centers are controlled by LLMs. Recent work documents substantial intra-model repetition and inter-model homogeneity in LLM responses to open-ended prompts ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Although these findings concern generative behaviour rather than strategic governance, they raise the possibility that formally independent LLM centers may nevertheless respond similarly to the same incentives. A governance system may therefore be highly polycentric in its institutional structure while remaining behaviourally concentrated if its centers repeatedly make similar exploitation decisions or similar mistakes. Our theoretical results do not require behavioural heterogeneity across centers, but this distinction motivates our empirical examination of how language-model agents exercise authority under comparable strategic conditions, including whether different models exhibit similar exploitation decisions and reasoning patterns.

In this section, we study endogenous governance formation among large language model (LLM) agents. Our objective is to study whether polycentricity emerges naturally via their interactions, and whether the experimental results echo those of the theory developed in Section 3 . We start by describing the design of our simulation.

The simulations implement the reduced-form game of Section 3 , with perfect detection and compulsory exit following exploitation ( α = 1 \alpha=1 ). Agents can establish new centres, step down as centres, and voluntarily join or leave constituencies at governance transitions. At each transition, exploited delegates first leave their centres. Existing centres then decide whether to continue, remaining delegates decide whether to stay, and free agents may volunteer to become new centres. If multiple agents volunteer, one is selected uniformly at random. Once the set of centres is determined, free agents choose between individual control and delegation to an eligible centre. A departing delegate may volunteer during the same transition.

Agents know the governance rules and observe the public constituency structure and their own actions and outcomes, but not other agents’ private exploitation outcomes or reasoning. Each decision is accompanied by a history of the agent’s observations, organized by governance epoch. Model-generated explanations are recorded for analysis but are neither shared with other agents nor included in subsequent memory.

We ran five matched pairs of simulations, each with n = 30 n=30 GPT-6 Luna agents. Each pair compared two starting conditions. In the centralized initialization , one randomly selected agent began as the centre of a group containing all 30 agents. In the decentralized initialization , all agents began independently and could volunteer to become a centre. One volunteer was selected at random, and the other agents could choose whether to join. After initialization, both conditions followed the same governance rules described in the previous paragraph.

The two simulations in each pair shared the same random draws but used separate model calls and memories. Each pair used a different random seed. We set ( κ , ℓ , d , δ , L ) = ( 1 , 3 / 5 , 2 / 5 , 99 / 100 , 5 ) , (\kappa,\ell,d,\delta,L)=(1,3/5,2/5,99/100,5), which gives the theoretical benchmark interval 3 ≤ m ≤ 7 3\leq m\leq 7 for α = 1 \alpha=1 , according to Corollaries 2 and 5 . We use this interval to classify constituency sizes. Appendix C.1 has a detailed parameter sweep.

If an agent leaves a centre (e.g., due to exploitation), it cannot immediately rejoin. Before each later affiliation decision, the option to rejoin becomes available with probability 1 / 2 1/2 and remains available unless the agent rejoins and leaves again. Rejoining is always voluntary. Agents see which centres they can join, but do not know the reinstatement rule or its random outcomes. This mechanism captures membership renewal in a finite population of persistent agents. Without it, permanent restrictions on rejoining would gradually limit agents’ choices and could cause fragmentation unrelated to their strategic decisions. In real organizational settings, populations evolve as new members arrive and former members reconsider their affiliations. Probabilistic reinstatement provides an approximation of such membership renewal without introducing explicit population turnover, allowing constituencies to recover, reorganize, and compete for members over repeated governance epochs.

Each simulation contains 20 complete epochs. All agents received the same rules and one of five decision prompts: centre continuation, delegate release, volunteering, affiliation, or exploitation. Each prompt included the agent’s current observations, available actions, and private memory. We used GPT-6 Luna with medium reasoning effort and required agents to provide both a structured decision and a private explanation. All prompts are provided in Appendix C.3 , and the source code can be found in the supplement.

We call a constituency viable when m min ≤ m ≤ m max m_{\min}\leq m\leq m_{\max} , 1 1 1 This classification identifies constituency sizes satisfying the analytical bounds, rather than establishing that the centre behaves non-exploitatively. and an epoch polycentric when at least two viable constituencies coexist. For each operational round, we record each agent’s constituency size and whether they were exploited. To measure how cooperation gains are distributed, we compare each agent’s payoff with the independent-control payoff of − κ -\kappa and attribute the difference to centres or delegates according to their role.

For the pointwise comparison, Sol evaluated each post-initialization Luna decision state using the same rules, observations, available actions, and history, without seeing Luna’s decision or reasoning. Sol’s responses did not affect the Luna trajectories. We compared 4,551 volunteering decisions and 1,988 exploitation decisions across the two models. The five random seeds were independent, but decisions within each simulation were not; we therefore report the results descriptively. This comparison captures differences between the models in identical decision states, rather than outcomes from independently evolving Sol societies.

Luna agents repeatedly formed polycentric arrangements under both initialization conditions, but constituency membership remained fluid as fee-sharing incentives encouraged concentration and exploitation induced departures.

Although delegation generated organizational cost savings, centres captured most of these gains . This concentration was particularly pronounced under centralized initialization, where exploitation left delegates collectively worse off than under individual control.

Matched-state comparisons show that Luna and Sol were similarly willing to volunteer for leadership but differed substantially in their exploitation decisions and in the considerations emphasized in their explanations.

Polycentricity emerged through both formation and fragmentation. All ten trajectories became polycentric, in all ten episodes and in 117 of the 200 observed epochs. This occurred under both centralized (55/100 epochs) and decentralized (62/100 epochs) initialization. Each trajectory was polycentric in 8–15 of its 20 epochs. The routes to polycentricity differed markedly for each of the two initialization conditions (Figure 2 ). Across both conditions, constituencies repeatedly expanded beyond the analytical accountability bound, lost members, and re-formed around existing or new centres. Thus,the agents did not simply select and maintain a partition within the theoretically compatible interval; polycentricity emerged through an process of concentration, exploitation, exit, and reconstruction.

Table 2 compares the two initialization conditions across the full trajectories. Decentralized initialization produced slightly more polycentric epochs (62% versus 55%) and greater agent-round exposure to constituencies within the theoretical size interval (29.2% versus 24.6%). More importantly, exploitation exposure after the first epoch was lower (42.2% versus 52.9%). These descriptive differences suggest that the initial distribution of authority may influence subsequent governance dynamics, even though both conditions generated repeated formation and fragmentation of constituencies.

Exploitation often triggered the departure of targeted delegates, however these losses were not necessarily permanent: centres could attract new delegates, and departed agents could regain the opportunity to rejoin. Indeed, some centre explanations explicitly anticipated membership recovery when deciding whether to exploit .

Every trajectory remained polycentric for at least two consecutive epochs, and one did so for ten. Some constituencies even grew to 14 agents, way above the theoretical bound. Nevertheless, larger constituencies subsequently fragmented, while smaller constituencies repeatedly lost members to competing centres. The observed dynamics were therefore characterized by recurring concentration, exploitation, exit, and re-formation, rather than convergence to a persistent governance structure.

Although fee sharing creates aggregate gains relative to individual control, exploitation can redistribute these gains from delegates to centres. To examine who benefits from delegation, we measured each agent’s payoff gain relative to independent control and aggregate these gains separately for centres and delegates.

For the centralized initialization, centres captured 104.4 % 104.4\% of aggregate delegation surplus, leaving delegates with a negative share of − 4.4 % -4.4\% . A share exceeding 100 % 100\% is possible – i.e., delegates can be collectively worse off than under independent control – because exploitation transfers payoff from delegates to centres. Delegate surplus was negative in four of the five centralized repeats. For the decentralized initialization, centres captured 91.9 % 91.9\% of the surplus, while delegates retained 8.1 % 8.1\% , with positive delegate surplus in all five repeats. Thus, although centres received most of the organizational gains under both conditions, the distribution of these gains differed based on initial governance structures (see Appendix 6 ).

We next investigate whether agents’ governance decisions differ across models of varying capabilities. To this end, we compare a higher-capacity model (GPT-6 Sol) with a smaller model (GPT-6 Luna), evaluating their interest in assuming authority and their exploitation decisions under identical strategic conditions.

In 4,551 matched volunteering states, Luna and Sol volunteered in 96.53% and 99.17% of cases, respectively, agreeing in 96.04% of states. The difference was substantially larger for exploitation. In 1,988 matched centre-decision states, Sol initiated new exploitation 2 2 2 I.e., initiating exploitation of at least one additional delegate who was not previously being exploited during the current governance epoch. in 41.80% of cases, compared with 31.79% for Luna, a 10 percentage-points difference . The models agreed on whether to exploit in 65.74% of these states. This difference was particularly pronounced in the decentralized-initialization trajectories, where Sol exploited in 44.33 % 44.33\% of states compared with 28.11 % 28.11\% for Luna (a 16.23 16.23 percentage-point difference). In contrast, their exploitation rates were much closer in the centralized-initialization trajectories ( 38.64 % 38.64\% versus 36.38 % 36.38\% , respectively). These results suggest that willingness to assume a leadership role provides little information about how an agent will exercise authority once that role has been acquired.

Figure 3 compares the models’ exploitation decisions across constituency sizes. Within the theoretical benchmark interval ( 3 ≤ m ≤ 7 3\leq m\leq 7 ), Sol initiated exploitation in 31.46 % 31.46\% of matched states, compared with 20.76 % 20.76\% for Luna. Above the accountability threshold ( m > 7 m>7 ), these rates increased to 44.00 % 44.00\% and 28.00 % 28.00\% , respectively. Moreover, Sol continued to target a similar proportion of delegates in larger constituencies, whereas Luna targeted a smaller proportion (see also Appendix 7 ).

Furthermore, the models differed not simply in their willingness to exploit, but in how they assessed its longer-term consequences . To investigate these differences, we analysed the transcripts using Non-negative Matrix Factorisation (NMF) ( Lee and Seung, 1999 ) to identify four recurring themes in the models’ written explanations (see Appendix C.2 ). In the 440 matched states where Sol exploited but Luna did not, Luna placed much greater emphasis on the future fee increases caused by losing delegates (the mean normalized weight assigned to long-term fee loss was 67.3 % 67.3\% for Luna and 3.3 % 3.3\% for Sol). Conversely, Sol emphasized the possibility that departing constituents would soon be replaced, either by returning members or by new delegates, allowing the centre to maintain its constituency size (64.5% versus 15.0% for Luna). These differences relate to accountability: departure disciplines a centre only when the resulting membership loss is sufficiently durable. Luna’s explanations primarily represented departure as a future fee cost, whereas Sol’s more often represented it as turnover that could be offset by retained or replacement members. Nevertheless, note that these findings describe differences in the models’ generated explanations, rather than establishing what caused their decisions.

Sol exploited more frequently, while Luna targeted more delegates when it did exploit. Conditional on initiating exploitation, Luna targeted 81.57 % 81.57\% of eligible delegates, compared with 74.25 % 74.25\% for Sol. However, because Sol initiated exploitation more frequently, it selected more new targets per decision on average ( 1.011 1.011 versus 0.670 0.670 ). The models also differed in timing (Figure 4 ). Their exploitation rates were similar in the first operational round, but, counter-intuitively, Sol was more likely to initiate exploitation of additional delegates in subsequent rounds, particularly rounds two to four. This is in contrast to Lemma 7 , which establishes that exploitation is more beneficial to the center at the beginning of an epoch, since the centre can benefit from it for the greatest number of remaining rounds.

These findings also illustrate the distinction between structural polycentricity and behavioural diversity discussed in Section 3.5 . Even when centres face identical strategic conditions, the model controlling them can influence their exploitation decisions and their assessment of future membership losses. Thus, distributing decision-making power across multiple centres does not, by itself, determine how those centres will behave. Our matched-state comparison demonstrates behavioural differences across model families, although it does not establish whether centres controlled by the same model make correlated decisions.

Our theoretical and empirical results highlight a central tension in delegated governance: the economies of scale that encourage agents to form larger constituencies can also weaken the accountability of their centres. The theory identifies a minimum size at which delegation becomes individually attractive and a maximum size at which the threat of individual exit can deter exploitation. However, this is a feasibility result, not a prediction that agents will form or maintain such a partition. In fact, in the simulations, while polycentric arrangements emerged under both initialization conditions, constituencies repeatedly grew, fragmented, and re-formed.

A key insight concerns the robustness of exit as an accountability mechanism . In the simulations, exploited delegates always leave at the next governance transition, but centres may subsequently attract replacement members. Thus, even certain departure does not necessarily provide a strong deterrent when the resulting membership loss may be temporary. This helps explain why exploitation can persist in real life despite compulsory exit and why constituencies may grow beyond the theoretical accountability threshold.

Our results also distinguish the efficiency of delegation from the distribution of its benefits . Sharing organizational costs generates aggregate gains, but exploitation allows centres to appropriate those gains at their delegates’ expense. Indeed, following centralized initialization, delegates were collectively worse off than under independent control, despite positive aggregate delegation surplus. Delegates fared better under decentralized initialization, although centres still captured most of the gains. These findings suggest that the emergence of collective institutions, or even multiple competing institutions, is not by itself sufficient evidence that delegation benefits those who surrender control.

Finally, the comparison between Luna and Sol illustrates one element of why structural polycentricity should be distinguished from behavioural diversity. The models were similarly willing to become centres but differed substantially in their exploitation decisions, even when presented with identical strategic states. The behaviour of the models exercising authority matters alongside the institutional structure in which they operate.

We studied how economies of scale and exit-based accountability shape voluntary delegation to self-interested centres. Our theory identifies the constituency sizes at which delegation is attractive and exploitation can be deterred, and characterizes when fully delegated accountable governance must be polycentric. Simulations with LLM agents show that polycentric arrangements repeatedly emerge, but remain fluid as constituencies expand, exploit, lose members, and re-form. They also reveal that centres can capture most of the gains from delegation, and that different language models may exercise identical authority in substantially different ways.

Together, these findings suggest that distributing authority across multiple centres is not sufficient to ensure accountable governance. What matters is whether exit imposes meaningful costs on those exercising authority, and how those agents respond to these incentives. Beyond these findings, our reduced-form environment can serve as a benchmark for the multi-agent systems community, enabling researchers to systematically compare AI agents and governance mechanisms under different incentives for delegation, exploitation, and exit.

We analyzed the 3,976 explanations from all 1,988 post-initialization exploitation-state pairs. Agent identifiers and numeric magnitudes were masked before TF–IDF vectorization with unigrams and bigrams. We fitted a four-component non-negative matrix factorization with seed 2027; model identity and action were not inputs. We named each component from its highest-weight terms and inspected the three matched pairs with the largest absolute model difference for that component. Topic weights were normalized to sum to one within each explanation.
